Comparative advantages and limitations of g-\( C_3N_4 \) relative to other photocatalytic nanomaterials

Comparative advantages and limitations of g-\( C_3N_4 \) relative to other photocatalytic nanomaterials

The development of nanophotocatalysts for cancer therapy has expanded beyond conventional metal-oxide semiconductors to include two-dimensional materials, carbon-based nanomaterials, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), and other multifunctional nanoplatforms. Representative systems include \( TiO_2 \) and \( ZnO \), graphene oxide (GO), black phosphorus (BP), transition-metal dichalcogenides such as \( MoS_2 \), MXenes, and MOFs. These materials possess distinct optical, electronic, catalytic, and surface properties that can be advantageous for photodynamic, photothermal, chemodynamic, drug-delivery, or multimodal cancer therapy. Therefore, positioning g-\( C_3N_4 \) within this broader nanomaterial landscape is important for defining both its advantages and its current limitations.

Compared with these 2D materials, g-\(C_{3}N_{4}\) offers a different functional advantage as a metal-free semiconductor with intrinsic photocatalytic redox activity and a readily tunable electronic structure. Thus, rather than universally outperforming other 2D materials, g-\(C_{3}N_{4}\) may be particularly advantageous when photocatalytic ROS generation and interfacial redox reactions are prioritized, whereas materials such as borophene and black phosphorus may offer stronger NIR photothermal responses. Integrating g-\(C_{3}N_{4}\) with complementary 2D materials may therefore provide a rational strategy for combining photocatalytic, photoelectric, and photothermal functionalities.

Photocatalytic mechanisms for cancer therapy

Reactive oxygen species generation

The photocatalytic activity of \( \mathrm{g}-\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4} \)-based nanomaterials is primarily associated with their ability to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) under appropriate light irradiation [59]. Upon absorption of photons with energies exceeding the effective bandgap, electrons are promoted from the valence band (VB) to the conduction band (CB), leaving photogenerated holes in the VB. The subsequent generation, migration, separation, and interfacial transfer of these charge carriers determine both the quantity and chemical identity of the ROS produced at the nanomaterial–biological interface [60].

Importantly, the therapeutic consequences of ROS generation depend not only on the total ROS level but also on ROS identity, lifetime, diffusion range, and subcellular site of formation.

Abstract
Cancer remains one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, necessitating the development of more precise
and effective therapeutic strategies. Graphitic carbon nitride (\( g\text{-}C_3N_4 \)) has emerged as a highly promising metal-free
semiconductor nanomaterial for photocatalytic cancer therapy owing to its tunable bandgap (\(\sim\)2.7 eV), favorable
biocompatibility, chemical stability and large surface area. Recent advances in nanotechnology and surface

Biosafety and in vivo validation

Although \( \mathrm{g}-\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4} \) has shown promising biocompatibility in several experimental systems, its long-term safety profile remains insufficiently established for clinical translation. Important considerations include biodistribution, tissue accumulation, degradation or clearance, immune responses, organ toxicity, and the potential toxicity of dopants, metal components, or surface coatings [131]. Moreover, the biological behavior of engineered \( \mathrm{g}-\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4} \) can differ substantially from that of pristine material. Comprehensive pharmacokinetic, toxicological, and long-term in vivo studies are therefore required before claims regarding clinical safety can be substantiated.

A schematic illustration summarizing the major challenges and future development directions of \( \mathrm{g}-\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4} \)-based nanoplatforms in cancer therapy is presented in Fig. 5. The major challenges include limited light penetration, tumor hypoxia, elevated intracellular GSH, limited tumor targeting and penetration, biosafety concerns, and difficulties in scalable and reproducible synthesis. Emerging strategies include NIR/NIR-II-responsive architectures, oxygen self-supplying and oxygen-independent catalytic pathways, GSH-regulating systems, multifunctional theranostic platforms, advanced targeting approaches, and AI-assisted nanomaterial design. Collectively, these approaches may improve the therapeutic precision, biological safety, and translational potential of \( \mathrm{g}-\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4} \)-based nanoplatforms.

Therefore, rational electronic engineering should simultaneously consider bandgap energy, band-edge positions, defect-state distribution, charge-carrier lifetime, interfacial charge transfer, and redox potentials [23]. These considerations are particularly important for g-\(C_{3}N_{4}\)-based photocatalytic cancer therapy, because therapeutic efficacy depends not simply on light absorption but also on efficient charge-carrier separation, lifetime, and interfacial transfer. Accordingly, rational electronic-structure engineering provides an important basis for optimizing the photophysical and interfacial properties of g-\(C_{3}N_{4}\), while the subsequent charge-transfer pathways and ROS-generation mechanisms are discussed in Section “Photocatalytic mechanisms for cancer therapy”.
